title: The HANDS Framework

keyTerms.d: A memory device coined by Robert M. Bowman Jr. and J. Ed Komoszewski: the New Testament presents Jesus as sharing five things that belong to God alone — Honors (the honors due to God), Attributes (the attributes of God), Names (the names of God), Deeds (the deeds only God does), and Seat (the seat of God’s throne).

Bauckham’s thesis is that Second Temple Jews defined their one God not chiefly by abstract attributes but by identity — he alone created all things, he alone rules all things, he alone bears the divine name, he alone is worshiped. That reading is widely influential, though the divine identity category is itself debated.

The Jewish principle of agency: “a man’s agent is as the man himself.” An ambassador is honored, obeyed, and received as though he were the king — without being the king. It is the key tool of those who affirm the Bible but deny that Jesus is God by nature.

keyTerms.t: Homage vs. the substance of worship
keyTerms.d: A gesture of homage was not itself the line: Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD — 1 Chronicles 29:20 uses a single verb of prostration for both. What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer.

“Lord.” The Greek Old Testament used Kyrios to render the divine name YHWH, and New Testament writers repeatedly take such YHWH texts and apply them to Jesus (Phil. 2:10–11 with Isa. 45:23; Rom. 10:13 with Joel 2:32).

Where a single article governs two singular, personal nouns joined by “and” that are not proper names (“God and Savior”), the two normally refer to one person — the most natural reading of Titus 2:13, “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,” and of 2 Peter 1:1. Whether Titus 2:13 calls Jesus “God” still turns on Greek grammar and remains debated.

The worry, rooted in Cullmann, that the New Testament speaks of what Jesus does, not of his eternal nature. The distinction is real; but the functions the New Testament assigns Jesus are functions Jewish monotheism reserved to God’s being. The function presupposes the identity.

The case does not rest on one verse or one line, but on the way five independent strands — honors, attributes, names, deeds, seat — all point in the same direction across documents written by different authors in different decades. Its strands cannot be neutralized all at once.

derive.q: Paul writes that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” — words YHWH speaks in the very chapter where he declares “I am the LORD, and there is no other” (Isa. 45:23, 45:5) — so Paul has…?
derive.ans: applied the most exclusive claim in the Hebrew Bible to Jesus (how specifically, debated)
derive.why: He took language from the most jealously exclusive claim in the Hebrew Bible and applied it to a crucified Galilean. That Philippians 2:11 applies YHWH language specifically, rather than “Lord” more generally, is itself a contested point among interpreters.

derive.q: Revelation twice has an angel refuse worship with “Worship God!” — yet every creature sings the same blessing “to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” — so…?
derive.ans: the Lamb receives what the angel forbids
derive.why: In Revelation 5:13–14 every creature sings to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb the same blessing and honor, and the elders fall down and worship — even though the same book twice has an angel refuse worship (Rev. 19:10; 22:9).

derive.q: Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD, with one verb for both (1 Chr. 29:20) — so the line Jewish monotheism guarded is…?
derive.ans: not the posture of homage but the substance of worship
derive.why: What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer. That is exactly why the angel in Revelation — himself God’s messenger — refuses the worship the Lamb accepts.

derive.q: Grant, for argument’s sake, that God’s name and authority could be entrusted to a supreme agent — what still could not be?
derive.ans: the worship, and the work of creation
derive.why: No shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic worship — offered to God, alongside God — that the New Testament gives Jesus; agency conferred authority, not that adoration. An agent represents the sender; he does not receive the sender’s worship, or do the sender’s unshareable work of creating all things (John 1:3; Col. 1:16).

derive.q: An Aramaic prayer, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Cor. 16:22), and a hymn applying an exclusive-worship text of YHWH to Jesus — so the highest devotion is…?
derive.ans: early, not late (the hymn’s pre-Pauline dating debated)
derive.why: Marana tha is a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, and Philippians 2 is widely regarded as a pre-Pauline hymn, within twenty-odd years of the crucifixion. The pre-Pauline dating is itself debated — Gordon Fee argues Paul composed the hymn — but the worship-of-Jesus datum stands either way.

derive.q: Dispute one finger — a contested grammar here, a milder rendering there — and what is left?
derive.ans: four strands, each demanding its own explanation
derive.why: A different reason the man receives worship, a different reason he bears the Name, a different reason he shares the one throne, a different reason he does the Creator’s unshareable works. A single ambiguity is cheap to absorb; a different ad hoc account for each of five independent strands is not.

honestState.p1: It would be triumphalist to claim the matter is closed. The “divine identity” reading associated with Bauckham is widely influential, though the divine identity category is itself debated: Hurtado reads the same data as a pattern of devotion, James F. McGrath disputes the category outright, and Dunn continued to press a more cautious line to the end. A minority of scholars still favor a more developmental or adoptionist account of the earliest period. No single HANDS finger, pressed alone, will compel a determined skeptic.
honestState.fairness: Individual proof-texts remain debated: whether Titus 2:13 and Romans 9:5 call Jesus “God” turns on Greek grammar; whether 1 Corinthians 8:6 folds Jesus into the Shema or instead sets a distinct “Lord” beside the one God is pressed by critics such as McGrath; whether Philippians 2 quotes YHWH specifically, or “Lord” more loosely, is disputed. Much New Testament language about Jesus’ being “given,” “sent,” and “appointed” does fit the agency reading naturally — but the agency category explains the sending; it breaks at the altar — and one cannot read Chalcedon’s metaphysics straight off the page of Mark.
honestState.verdict: The HANDS framework is not a single mathematical proof of the Trinity, and it should not be sold as one; nor can it force assent from someone committed to a unitarian reading of every passage. What it does establish is that the New Testament — read in its own first-century Jewish context — presents Jesus of Nazareth as sharing the honors, attributes, names, deeds, and throne of the one God of Israel, and does so early, pervasively, and on purpose. So the verdict this evidence supports is plain: Jesus is God. The gospel needs him to be, and joyfully confesses him to be, fully God and fully man.

order: Honors, Attributes, Names, Deeds, and Seat belong to God alone.
The New Testament deliberately attributes all five to Jesus.
Therefore the New Testament places Jesus within the unique identity of the one God.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Honors, Attributes, Names, Deeds, and Seat belong to God alone; even if name and authority could be delegated, the worship and the work of creation could not. Limit: the framework is not a single mathematical proof of the Trinity, and it should not be sold as one.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what kind of claim it is.
cards.a: The New Testament deliberately attributes all five to Jesus: he is worshipped, eternal, named with the divine Name, creator and final judge, and seated on God’s own throne. These are not, taken singly, knock-down proofs; the claim is cumulative and convergent.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the New Testament places Jesus within the unique identity of the one God: Jesus is God — fully God and fully man. It does not settle by itself every question of metaphysics the fourth-century councils would later define, nor force assent from someone committed to a unitarian reading of every passage.

cards.q: Why does the worship in Revelation carry weight?
cards.a: Every creature sings “to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” the same blessing and honor, and the elders fall down and worship — though the same book twice has an angel refuse worship with “Worship God!” The Lamb receives what the angel forbids.

cards.q: Where exactly is the line between homage and worship?
cards.a: Not the posture: Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD, with a single verb of prostration for both. What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer.

cards.q: Why does agency have a ceiling — and where is it?
cards.a: No shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic worship — offered to God, alongside God — that the New Testament gives Jesus; agency conferred authority, not that adoration. Grant that God’s name and authority could be entrusted to a supreme agent; the worship still could not be, and neither could the work of creation.

cards.q: Why are five strands harder to dismiss than one?
cards.a: Dispute one finger and four remain, each demanding its own separate explanation. The one unifying alternative — that all five are the dignity of a supreme agent — has already run aground on the worship the Lamb receives, which agency never conferred.

cards.q: What does 1 Corinthians 8:6 do with the Shema — and how secure is that reading?
cards.a: It appears to split the Shema, not demote the Son: “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” — “Lord” being the divine Name, setting Jesus within Israel’s confession of the one God, not beside it. That reading is influential, arguably dominant, and genuinely contested.

cards.q: Reply to: sitting at God’s right hand means NOT being God.
cards.a: Two persons, certainly — that is Trinitarianism, not a problem for it. A viceroy may be seated beside a king, and by the king’s grant may even share his rule; what no viceroy receives is that worship. Revelation pictures one throne of God and of the Lamb, before which the redeemed render undivided worship.

cards.q: Reply to: but Jesus grows, prays, and does not know the hour.
cards.a: The New Testament holds both halves on purpose, often in one breath — the upholder of the universe “made purification for sins” (Heb. 1:3). The counter-lines describe what the Son took on; the HANDS lines describe what he never ceased to be.

cards.q: Functional, not ontological — what is conceded, and what is the reply?
cards.a: Conceded: the distinction is real, the New Testament’s idiom is largely functional, and Nicaea’s vocabulary of “essence” is later. Reply: creating the world, ruling from the one throne, receiving worship, bearing the Name are functions Jewish monotheism reserved to God’s being. The function presupposes the identity.

cards.q: The developmental objection — what does it say developed, and what answers it?
cards.a: It claims two lines of development: in exaltation Christologies the moment Jesus became Son was pushed back from resurrection to baptism to birth; in incarnation Christologies what developed was not the date of pre-existence but the pre-existent figure’s rank — conceived at first as a subordinate divine being, whose elevation to the co-equal God is the later step. Answer: the earliest worship already placed Jesus inside the one God’s identity, not beneath it as a lesser divinity. No Jewish writer we know of wrote a second figure into the creed of divine uniqueness itself (Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and it is never placed inside that confession); Paul did — on a reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6 that is influential and genuinely contested. So at the point that matters, we judge that the developmental thesis does not hold.

obj.q: Worship just means homage — people bowed to kings too. Proskuneo is used of bowing to human authorities throughout the ancient world. Honors prove etiquette, not deity.
obj.model: A gesture of homage was not itself the line: Israelites could bow before a king as well as before the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:20). What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer. That is exactly why the angel in Revelation — himself God’s messenger — refuses the worship the Lamb accepts. Peter refuses Cornelius’s worship (“I too am a man”), and Revelation’s angel refuses it twice (“Worship God!”). The risen Jesus accepts it, in heaven, from every creature, alongside the One on the throne. The same documents that police the line for men and angels watch Jesus stand on the far side of it.

obj.q: In the Hebrew Bible an emissary bears the sender’s name and authority — the angel of the LORD speaks as God, Moses is made “like God to Pharaoh” — and Jewish law put it as the shaliach principle: a man’s agent is as the man himself. So Jesus is God’s supreme agent, given the divine name, the divine works, and a relative honour, while remaining a distinct and subordinate being. Your own evidence says he was sent, given, appointed. That is agent language.
obj.model: The agency motif really is there — the sent/given/appointed language fits it naturally, and that should be granted. But it breaks at one point. A gesture of homage was never the line: Israelites bowed before a king and before the LORD with the same verb (1 Chronicles 29:20). What Jewish monotheism guarded for God alone was the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer. Angels, prophets and kings could be honoured; none of them could be prayed to. And in 1 Corinthians 16:22 Paul, writing Greek to a Greek city, leaves one Aramaic phrase untranslated: Marana tha — “Our Lord, come!” That is prayer, addressed to Jesus, originating among the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers in Judea. A figure you worship and pray to, while confessing in the same breath that God is one, has already outrun the category of supreme agent. Nor does an agent do the sender’s unshareable work of creating all things (John 1:3; Col. 1:16). The agency category explains the sending; it breaks at the altar.

obj.q: The historical Jesus did not claim to be God and was not worshiped as God in his lifetime. Christology developed along two lines: in exaltation Christologies the moment Jesus became Son was pushed back from resurrection to baptism to birth, while in incarnation Christologies the development was in the pre-existent figure’s rank: the earliest pre-existent Christ was a subordinate divine being, and his elevation to the co-equal God of Nicaea came later. The loftiest texts — “I am,” Thomas’s confession, the shared throne — are the church’s later theology read back onto Jesus.
obj.model: The strongest evidence is the one thing the developmental thesis cannot easily accommodate: the earliest worship. Philippians 2 already applies an exclusive-worship text of YHWH to Jesus (its pre-Pauline dating is itself debated, but the worship-of-Jesus datum stands either way), and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha is a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church. Wisdom is praised; Enoch is exalted; but no Jewish writer we know of wrote a second figure into the creed of divine uniqueness itself (Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and it is never placed inside that confession). Paul did — on the reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6 that is influential, arguably dominant, and genuinely contested. So at the point that matters, we judge that the developmental thesis does not hold: on that reading, which we take to be the right one, the earliest devotion already placed Jesus inside the one God’s identity, not beneath it as a lesser divinity.

obj.q: Your five lines collide with five counter-lines: ignorance, fatigue, prayer, death. Honest reading says the New Testament is conflicted about Jesus, and you have curated one half.
obj.model: The New Testament itself holds both halves on purpose — often in the same breath: the Creator of all things “became flesh”; the one in the form of God “emptied himself”; the upholder of the universe “made purification for sins” (Hebrews 1:3 — one verse, both truths). That is not editorial confusion; it is the doctrine of the incarnation, stated before any council named it. The counter-lines describe what the Son took on; the HANDS lines describe what he never ceased to be — and a reading that keeps every text beats a reading that must delete half of them.

unseen.q: Pre-existence is only in John. Mark, Matthew and Luke never present a Son who was there before he came — their Jesus speaks like any prophet on a mission.
unseen.model: Even in the Synoptic Gospels Jesus speaks as one who has come — “the Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45); “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10); “I have come to bring fire on the earth” (Luke 12:49). Simon Gathercole argues that this “I have come” idiom is the speech of one announcing the purpose of his coming — the form used, in Jewish writings, of a heavenly figure sent on a mission. That is a parallel of form, not of nature: it does not say Jesus is an angel or a creature, for unlike any messenger this Son does the Father’s own works and receives the worship due God alone. The reading is contested — many take these sayings as ordinary language of prophetic mission (John the Baptist, too, “came,” Matt. 11:18), and Dunn holds that clear personal pre-existence appears only in John — so it is one convergent strand, not a proof. So the claim that pre-existence is only in John does not hold: even Ehrman finds a pre-existent Christ already in material older than Paul, and Bauckham insists the inclusion of Jesus in the unique divine identity occurs across the New Testament writings, not just John. Whether the Synoptic “I have come” sayings themselves carry pre-existence stays contested, and the case does not hang on them.
